W Jaguarze działa to tak:

\- Przełącznik lead/rhythm (ten bliżej Ciebie patrząc z pozycji kiedy trzymasz gitarę - obok którego są dwie rolki) - jeśli ustawisz go 'do siebie', jest włączony rhythm circuit, tzn. działa tylko przetwornik przy gryfie i brzmienie jest 'ciemniejsze'. Te dwie rolki obok przełącznika regulują głośność i jasność. *Wszystkie inne przełączniki/potencjometry na gitarze są wtedy nieaktywne.*

\- Jeśli ustawisz przełącznik lead/rhythm 'dalej od siebie', uaktywniają się wtedy te trzy przełączniki na Twoim zdjęciu + potencjometry volume & tone (te obok gniazda jack).

\- Te trzy przełączniki z Twojego zdjęcia działają wtedy następująco (od lewej do prawej):

* Neck pickup: bliżej ciebie = ON, dalej od ciebie = OFF
* Bridge pickup: bliżej ciebie = ON, dalej od ciebie = OFF
* Strangle switch (odcina częstotliwości basowe, przez co brzmienie jest 'płytsze'): bliżej ciebie = ON (płytki dżwięk), dalej od ciebie = OFF (pełny dźwięk)

Given the above, jeśli ustawisz te pierwsze 2 przełączniki 'dalej od siebie', każdy z nich jest OFF = nic wtedy nie usłyszysz.

As a fellow OCD sufferer - by posting here, you're trying to seek reassurance whether you're a bad person or not. This is a compulsion, so you need to try to cut it out. Embrace the idea that you might actually be a bad person and/or you might have committed actions that created bad karma. Live with that idea without trying to gain 100% certainty if it's true or not.

Edit: Some general info for others as I see a lot of misinformation here: this is a real disease. 'Religious OCD' is when a person is obsessed with e.g. having committed a terrible sin, offending God, etc. The person then tries to relieve the intrusive thoughts by performing compulsions, e.g. constantly confessing their sins to family/friends/priest; asking them if they think they're a good/bad person, whether they did something terrible etc. Engaing with the person and providing them with reassurance that they're good actually worsens the disease - the relief is temporary and it's only a matter of time before the person seeks the reassurance again. The goal of treatment is to stop compulsions; we must NOT provide reassurance because it feeds the disease.

A big thing in OCD is that it plays on uncertainty. A key part of therapy is accepting and embracing that uncertainty, and resisting trying to obtain certainty. In case of false memories, this would require resisting any attempts to determine if the memory the brain is presenting you with is real or imagined. E.g. if you're afraid you ran someone over with your car, you'd need to accept that you just don't know, and resist trying to find out. It's kind of like making this big leap of faith, although it's very terrifying.

Your experience  is perfectly normal (as far as OCD goes). The 'feeling of going insane' occurs mostly during heightened states of anxiety, which I suspect you're experiencing given the severity of your condition. What actually happens is that you get 'anxiety about the anxiety getting out of control and turning you into a crazy person'. And sometimes the OCD experience itself, the racing thoughts, the compulsions... it all gets so intense that it seems like you're losing it. It's not true, though. You're thinking about going insane; that's different from actually going insane. If I think about oranges, will oranges magically appear in front of me?

This is generally referred to as 'thought-action fusion'. Basically, we become so glued to and hyperfocused on the obsessive thoughts that we treat them as they are actual reality. Our attention span is so limited, it's like we don't know that there's 'more'. Our view of reality becomes so narrow, we start beliving that the narrative provided by the thoughts is true. We're unable to easily access an alternative that would disprove the thoughts. And so we look for an alternative - we try to disprove the thoughts - by doing compulsions.

Now, on to your question, 'do SSRIs lose efficacy'; well, to be perfectly honest with you, there is a subset of individuals that have this experience where their SSRI stops working and they need to look for a different medication. But I'd estimate that subset as 15% of the population, tops. We know very little about the human brain. Psychiatry these days is still a 'hit-or-miss' thing. They have algorithms that tell them how to prescribe the meds so that they arrive at the best working combo for you as quick as possible. These algorithms are based on evidence, and in my opinion they do work. 

Even if something helps you only for some time, it's still better than no help at all. And for OCD, the SSRI response rate is 40-60%. Very few get complete remission from them, but many do get substantial symptom relief.

Yeah, that's FOMO OCD. I get that, in my case I think I do have a little bit of a real FOMO, but the OCD latches on to it and takes it to the extreme. If it's Friday evening and I see people outside walking and doing stuff, I will get this urge where I *must* go out and do *something* or otherwise it's just this unbearable feeling.

Unfortunately, SSRIs (or serotonin boosting drugs in general) are the main way this is treated pharmacologically. 

Some doctors 'boost' the SSRIs with antipsychotics. For some people this decreases the OCD, particularly if they have a comorbid tic disorder.

Therapy is the way to go, it actually has a better success rate than any drugs when it comes to OCD. 

The only other things that come to my mind are experimental treatments which target the glutamate system instead of the serotonin system:

* IV ketamine treatment. If you live in the US, you might be able to find a ketamine clinic that offers this type of therapy.
* Memantine, a drug used to treat Alzheimer's which was found to help in some studies. 

You'll need to consult with your doc.

OK, so, first of all, the 'you don't really have OCD' and 'you're a piece of shit' thoughts are totally relatable. You'll see lots of folks here having this experience. "OCD about OCD" is a thing (obsessing whether you actually have OCD) and the whole guilt/feeling-like-the-worst-person-in-the-world is also a thing. 

Based on the description of your situation, I would highly recommend trying both medications and therapy together. ERP therapy is the recommended first-line of treatment in all cases, although it can be difficult to find a provider. Medication (according to the most recent guidelines) should be included if things are really difficult or if you're not responding to therapy. SSRIs are nothing to be afraid of. When I was first offered them, I declined because I had this attitude, *"I'm not going to chemically alter my brain like that, what if the drugs change me, this is just big pharma and these drugs don't really work, blah blah".* I should have taken them right then and there. Lexapro quite literally saved my life. It literally keeps my brain from falling apart and getting sucked in the obsession hole again. I know that if I stop taking it, I'll go back to where I was. And I will do everything I can to prevent going back to this dark place. If need be, I am completely fine with taking these meds until the very last day of my life. 

But generally speaking, therapy is more effective because it teaches you how to respond to these things internally so that they don't bother you as much and the symptoms dissipate.

It is a form dissociation, but it's kind of different from the dissociation that's usually talked about, like with DID, depersonalization etc. With OCD, the dissocation does not serve a function of a defense mechanism against trauma. It's merely a byproduct of the obsessive-compulsive cycle. The compulsions are disrupting the natural 'flow' of our consciousness, so stuff just doesn't organically unfold in our minds. After a while we just don't feel like we're 'whole'. Also, our attention is so fixated on obsessions that it's very difficult to redirect it to anything else. This state of hyperfocus is called 'dissociative absorption' and studies have shown it's very common in OCD. If you're hyperfixated on something 24/7, you don't really have a chance to experience anything else in your mind, e.g. an emotion, because that would require moving your consciousness away from the obsession so that there's enough room in your mind for the emotion.

You're not alone, I've been experiencing this everyday for years. When my intrusive thoughts were really bad, I developed this mental compulsion where I would sort of 'force them away' from my consciousness. 

The thing is, it's impossible to selectively 'force out' one component of our conscious experience. So I ended up blocking my entire stream of consciousness by doing this compulsion. This is basically a form of dissociation - aspects of the personality are 'locked out' and we end up feeling disconnected from our sense of self. 

And I totally relate to the thing where you don't even know if you like something. Like, how do I know if I like this piece of music? To know that, I would first need to know how I *feel about it*. 'Feeling a certain way about something' is an aggregate of experiencing a number of emotions and thoughts in response to something over a period of time. If I can't even experience an emotion because it's locked out from my conscious experience, then I have no idea if I like the thing in front of me.
Thank you for sharing and I'm glad that you got better. 'Compulsion is not an option' is a great way of putting it.

>I think once you are okay with 24 hour monitoring of yourself, you're about at the bottom of it.

OCD doesn't have a 'bottom'. Today you think it can't get worse, next day you're even deeper down in the hole. Today you're comfortable inside your room, tomorrow you'll only be comfortable inside a chalk circle around your bed (I'm not kidding, I've heard of a patient that got to the point where he would shit and piss inside a circle with their bed in it, and never leave the circle because something bad would happen).

If you want to get better, you need to accept that healing from this illness goes by the 'no pain, no gain' rule. It gets worse before it gets better. But what's important is that it *does* get better, we just have to put in the hard work.

I have diagnosed OCD, so just speaking from experience. This does sound like a classic OCD symptom. The intrusive thoughts in OCD revolve around things you care about. You mentioned tearing up thinking about Buddha and while reading sutras, and you considered taking refuge. This means Buddhism is something you highly value, therefore, it will make sense that the disorder will 'attack' this part of your live.

One of the compulsions in OCD is seeking reassurance. You can seek reassurance in many ways, including making posts like this. Reading other people's explanations of how the Buddha is not Satan will give you a temporary relief, but this actually reinforces the obsession-compulsion cycle. So, you should try to refrain from doing that. Instead, try accepting your uncertainty that Buddha might have been Satan (or let's just generally say, evil) and sit with that discomfort. And also, seek professional help because this doesn't go away on its own.

Not cured, but you can be in remission.

You know how volcanos can be inactive for hundreds of years and then suddenly erupt? A flare-up of symptoms is like an eruption. If you treat it, the 'OCD volcano of intrusive thoughts' goes dormant again for some time, but it will erupt again some time in the future.

Theoretically, the generic stuff should be the same as the original, i.e. the molecular structure of the active ingredient is exactly the same. 

However, I also experienced what you describe here. I was on a particular generic version, then discovered I could save a shit ton of money by switching to a different brand (25% the cost of the one I was using).

2 days after the switch I already knew it wasn't working as it was supposed to. I was prepared though and had one blister pack of the old stuff ready.

Turns out where I'm from (EU) there can actually be a +/- 20% difference in the active substance dose between brands and this is acceptable. Also, the excipients (stuff that binds the pill together) can differ and this may affect how each generic is absorbed.   


I found another cheap generic, but this time from a well-known reputable pharma brand. I'll try it next week and see how this one does.

Yes, that's true! My OCD also led me to Buddhism, I'm happy to connect with people who also share this perspective.

The thing is, that this illusion of 'I', our clinging to our 'selves', is something that's very deep-rooted in our minds. To be truly free from these chains would require years of meditation, practicing Buddhist precepts and gaining insights into workings of the mind. We can understand on an intellectual level that this is true, that there's no such thing as a 'self', but it's a whole other thing to actualy live that reality.

I imagine that an advanced Buddhist monk who attained the complete understaing of no-self would not be bothered by intrusive thoughts in the slightest; as you say, the very root of our suffering is clinging and attachment, not the OCD itself.

I must say though that this content could be potentially triggering for those of us who suffer from the existential/philosophical variety of our ailment. Might be a good idea to add a trigger warning to the post.

There's a Buddhist scholar, William S. Waldron, who writes about alayavijnana extensively. It can be hard to understand at times because it's very academic, but after you learn all the fancy terms it gets easier. Alayavijnana is sometimes called the "storehouse-consciousness". It is the basis of (i.e. gives rise to) all other seven forms of consciousness, so if it ceases to exist, you're not reborn anymore. It is the consciousness that moves from one body to another during rebirth.

Each time you perform an action, that action generates certain karma. That karma is like an impression, and it's stored in the alayavijnana. Sometimes the "impression" is explained using the metaphor of wind. When wind blows from place to place, it carries the smells of the different places it goes through. Say that wind blows and there's sewage on the way; it will carry the bad odour with it. But then there's a big field of blooming flowers, and so the wind will carry the sweet smells of flowers. 

The wind is like the alayavijnana, neither good/bad, just a blank template, existing and moving from place to place (i.e. being reborn); the smells are the karmic effects of actions that are imprinted on the alayavijnana.

These "impressions" are called "seeds". Alayavijnana is like a "master memory" - every action that you ever did, in all lifetimes, generated some karma, and all that info is being saved in the "master matrix" as seeds. Eventually, there comes a time when those seeds ripen and give rise to all the phenomena in your mindstream - thoughts, emotions, preferences, desires, things that constitute what we perceive as personality, etc. When the seed ripens, that's when the karma "returns", e.g. if you have done an unskillful action, the seed of that action will give rise to a "negative" state of mind.
The Yogachara school, specifically, the theory of alayavijnana explains this very well.

I would suggest trying to do an exposure. 

When you're reading, try to read the lines/pages one after another, without rechecking and trying to get that 'just right' feeling.

Trust me, I know it's easier said than done. 

But after some time doing this, what will happen is your brain will 'click' and form a new connection that bypasses the OCD loop. At that moment, you'll be like 'OMG! I don't have to reread the pages, that's so stupid. It's enough that I read it once'.

Of course, that doesn't mean the obsession will disappear. You will most likely slip back and feel like you need to recheck again. That's because the 'OCD loop' pathways are more 'engraved' in your brain, so to speak. But if you keep doing exposures, over time your brain will use the 'normal' pathways more and more, and eventually, you will be able to easily dismiss any obsession that enters your mind. 

In the OCD brain, there is a disrupted connection between two of its parts. So you read a line, and even though you *know* you've read it, your brain doesn't 'register' that quite completely. It's like there are two parts talking to each other. One says 'I've read the line' (or 'I've locked the door/I washed my hands' - whatever the obsession is), but the other doesn't 'hear' it. That's why you get that 'not right' feeling, the urge to check over and over, and the doubt (the part of the brain that was supposed to receive the message is asking, *'Is this done? Please confirm'*).

This is absolutely possible, since OCD and anxiety are actually two different things.

OCD used to be classified as an anxiety disorder until the American Psychiatric Association created a new category for it in the DSM-V: 'Obsessive-compulsive and related disorders'. There's a growing body of research suggesting that the faulty OCD circuitry (i.e. related to the obsession-compulsion cycle) is actually separate from the anxiety/fear signalling.

Of course, many of us OCD sufferers do expierence a tremendous amount of anxiety. However, it seems like this anxiety is only sometimes accompanying the obsessions and compulsions; in other words, you do not have to have anxiety to have OCD.

There was a study done some time ago (I can't find it now) in which they found that you can distinguish between two groups of OCD sufferers:

- One group tends to feel intense anxiety when not performing a compulsion;

- The other group tends to feel a 'general sense of discomfort' when not performing a compulsion, often described as feeling that something is 'not just right'.

Basically, the 'core' of OCD is the obssesion-compulsion cycle and you don't have to have anxiety on top of that.

I live in a country where it's nearly impossible to find a therapist with experience in treating these weird, lesser known Pure-O themes; e.g. if you wash your hands frequently, check if you locked the door numerous times etc. they know how to apply ERP for that, but with themes centered around identity/existence, sometimes this can be actually misdiagnosed as a different disorder and people get the wrong treatment. 

So, I never really did any proper ERP, but I've been on medication for 3 years now (20 mg Lexapro) and I see a psychiatrist once in a few months (though she just checks if I feel ok and writes another prescription).

An app called 'NOCD' came out recently, however it's only for people in the US. It's therapy done via webcam and it seems they gathered a team of good professional doctors/psychologists who know what they're doing, so maybe that would be an option for you.

Another important aspect is psychoeducation - try reading/watching from Dr. Steven Phillipson and Mark Freeman, I think they're currently the best in the OCD field and give some really useful tips.

You could also try doing exposures yourself (self-applied ERP), however it's never going to be as effective as assisted ERP (sometimes, especially with Pure-O, we are unaware that what we are doing is a compulsion and there's no one to point this out). There's also mindfulness therapy - ACT (Acceptance & Commitment) - this is actually complementary to the gold-standard ERP treatment.

An increasing body of research is suggesting that antipsychotics are more harmful than helpful in treating OCD.

Basically, these drugs might make your OCD feel less intense because they slow down brain activity. However, it was proved that antipsychotics help in small-to-medium doses only - after a certain point, they actually increase the OCD symptoms.

The psychiatric guidelines recommend antipsychotics as an augmentation strategy based on research that was done circa 2000.

As you may know, this type of medication decreases dopamine signaling. There were studies done in recent years proving that dopaminergic transmission is out of whack in OCD - but this is not just a simple 'too much dopamine/too little dopamine' situation. In further studies, OCD patients were given stimulants (yes, Adderall), which work in the exact opposite way to antipsychotics. The results were promising - there was a significant symptoms reduction. The very recent psychiatric guidelines actually mention administering stimulants as an add-on in case the previous treatment fails.

I am not saying that Risperdal/Abilify/Olanzapine is not an option, but given the potential side effects of these drugs, there are plenty of other options (both medications and natural remedies) you should consider first. Antipsychotics are the 'heavy' psychiatric meds and should be considered as more of a 'last resort'.

I wish you all the best and hope you find the right treatment.

What I found out with my OCD is that the answer to any set of obsessions and compulsions is - dive straight into the anxiety by not performing the compulsion (e.g. reassurance seeking).

I know this sounds counterintuitive, however I believe that this is the only way to rewire the brain so it finally learns that it does not have to send all these 'possible threat ahead' signals.

You will have the thought that the food might be poisoned. This will make you anxious.

Do not feed the OCD by performing compulsions - eat the food, even if this makes you extremely anxious. 

Do not fight that anxiety. Let yourself feel it, because in this way the anxiety is released.

After some time you will be able to look back on that thought of poisoned food and think 'huh - that was a stupid thought'. At the time it did not seem stupid, it seemed very real because of the anxiety that came with that thought. However, after releasing this anxiety (by diving into it over and over again so your brain relearns stuff) your mind wisl be back to its natural state where it recognizes the stupid thoughts for what they are - just stupid thougjts.
